intro: Brussels is the rare city that has kept a formal, scientific register of its own remarkable trees since 2002, cataloguing more than a thousand specimens by age, rarity and historical weight. That bureaucratic thoroughness is why ages and girths on this list are unusually exact. It also explains an odd trick the city played on itself: when Brussels built the Cinquantenaire park in 1880 for Belgium's fiftieth anniversary, it did not plant saplings. It transplanted fully grown trees from an old cemetery and the edge of the Sonian Forest, so the new park looked centuries old on its opening day.
meta_description: Brussels has run an official register of its remarkable trees since 2002. Thirty verified locations, real stories, and how to reach each one.
question_answer: Brussels' oldest documented tree is the Chene Josephine, a pedunculate oak in Parc Jacques Brel in Forest, estimated at close to 400 years old from a trunk just over six metres around. Brussels' own heritage inventory calls it probably the oldest oak in the entire Brussels-Capital Region. It stands in a public park that only opened in 1980, though the tree itself long predates it.
question_meta: The Chene Josephine, a roughly 400 year old oak in Parc Jacques Brel, Forest, is Brussels' oldest documented tree. Where it stands, and twenty-nine more.
question_context: Chene Josephine's age comes from its girth rather than any planting record: at 6.05 metres in circumference, measured at chest height, foresters use growth-rate tables for pedunculate oak to arrive at a figure close to four centuries, old enough that Brussels' own heritage inventory calls it probably the oldest oak anywhere in the region. No document names a planting date, since the ground it grows on was still part of the Kersbeekbosch, a wood already recorded under that name in 1648, long before anyone thought to write down individual trees within it. The clearest challenger for oldest is the Kasterlinde, a lime tree marking the exact point where three communes meet, documented on maps since 1777 and therefore provably at least two and a half centuries old, though its estimated true age, worked out from girth, comes out younger than the oak's. Parc Jacques Brel itself is a recent public space, only opened by the commune of Forest in 1980 after decades as a private estate, but the oak inside it is the oldest living thing within reach of a Brussels metro station. It costs nothing to visit.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Brussels?
faq.a: Most likely the Chene Josephine, a pedunculate oak in Parc Jacques Brel, Forest, estimated at close to 400 years from its girth. Brussels' own heritage inventory calls it probably the oldest oak in the region.

faq.q: Are Brussels' remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all thirty stand in public parks, gardens and streets with no admission charge, unusual compared to cities where the oldest trees sit behind a castle or palace gate.

faq.q: Why does Brussels know so much about the age of its own trees?
faq.a: Since 2002, the region's heritage department has run a formal scientific inventory of remarkable trees, measuring circumference, checking rarity and recording historical association. That is why girths and ages here are unusually precise compared to most cities.

faq.q: Why are some of Brussels' most impressive trees not its oldest?
faq.a: Brussels has transplanted mature trees before rather than waiting for saplings to grow. When Parc du Cinquantenaire was built in 1880, city gardeners moved in fully grown trees from an old cemetery and the Sonian Forest, so several of its most striking trees are older than the park but younger than genuine centuries-old specimens elsewhere on this list.

trees.name: The Chene Josephine

location.address: Parc Jacques Brel, Avenue Besme, 1190 Forest, Brussels

trees.story: Brussels' own heritage inventory calls this oak probably the oldest tree of any kind in the entire region, and its evidence is a single number: 6.05 metres around the trunk, measured at chest height. That circumference translates, through standard oak growth tables, to an age close to four hundred years, since no planting record exists for a tree this old growing in what was once simply called the Kersbeekbosch, a wood already named in a document from 1648, a full century before anyone thought to record individual trees within it. A 20th century industrialist built a chateau and pleasure pavilion on the land and renamed it Parc des Eperons d'Or, but the commune of Forest only acquired the grounds in 1979 and opened them to the public in 1980, as Parc Jacques Brel. The oak, already three and a half centuries old by then, barely noticed the paperwork. At roughly 20 metres tall with a canopy shaped by centuries of unhurried growth, it now shares its park with joggers, a playground and Brussels' newer housing developments, a working class commune's public oak older than most of the buildings standing around it put together.

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Forest Centre, short walk into the park
trees.notes: Age is a girth-based estimate, not a documented planting date; the Kersbeekbosch reference (1648) establishes the wood existed, not this specific tree's age. Called 'probably the oldest oak' in the region by the Wood Wide Web heritage source, softened from an absolute claim per hard rule 8. No open licensed photo found this run. Pin was genuinely wrong, not just approximate: the stored coordinates sat about 1.5km from the actual park, seemingly a geocoding slip from an early research pass. Corrected 2026-07-27 directly from this entry's own already-cited source (woodwideweb.be's atlas entry for this exact tree, ID 1139, which states its own GPS reading), independently cross-checked against Nominatim's geocode of Parc Jacques Brel itself, which lands within 70m of the same point. Set to confirmed.

trees.name: The Kasterlinde

best_time.label: late June, when its flowers scent the whole street corner

location.address: Kasterlindenstraat, opposite Cafe In de Linde, Dilbeek, Brussels

trees.story: A single lime tree marks the exact spot where three Brussels communes meet, and it has been doing the job since at least 1777, when the Ferraris map, the first detailed survey of the Austrian Netherlands, recorded it at the boundary point of Molenbeek-Saint-Jean, Berchem-Sainte-Agathe and Dilbeek. Later maps track it by name: an 1821 survey shows it beside a chapel demolished that same decade, and an 1858 map of Brussels and its surroundings labels the spot simply Kaster Linde. Its trunk has thickened from 2.75 metres around in the early 1900s, when the Belgian botanist Chalon first measured it for his book on the country's trees, to 3.15 metres today, growth that puts its real age comfortably past two centuries even before the documentary trail is counted. A street and a nearby cafe, In de Linde, both take their name from it. Unlike a garden specimen chosen for its looks, this tree exists because generations of surveyors needed a fixed point that would not move, and a slow growing lime, marking a boundary since before Belgium existed as a country, turned out to be exactly that.
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: Bus to the Berchem-Sainte-Agathe / Dilbeek border

photo.attribution: Geert Van der Linden / Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Documentary trail (1777 Ferraris map, 1821 and 1858 surveys, Chalon's early 20th century measurement) is unusually solid for a single tree, corroborated across the official heritage inventory and an independent citizen blog. Photo verified on Commons: Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency's own inventory photo of the Dilbeek Kasterlindenstraat boundary tree, matching the described location precisely. Pin corrected 2026-07-28: the stored coordinate (50.8672, 4.2965) turned out to be about 1.3km from the real Kasterlindenstraat, discovered while Nominatim-geocoding the street named in this entry's own sources. Triangulated three independent ways: Kasterlindenstraat's own OSM geocode, neighbouring Kerselaarstraat's, and a direct name match for 'In De Linde' (a real cafe at 177 Kasterlindenstraat, exactly the landmark this entry's own story already names), all converging on the same spot. The heritage inventory page (inventaris.onroerenderfgoed.be/erfgoedobjecten/302035) confirms the crossroads/cemetery description but its own precise coordinate isn't exposed through this session's tooling; Brussels' own remarkable-tree register (sites.heritage.brussels) is blocked (403) for the same reason prior passes found, still true 2026-07-29. Resolved to confirmed 2026-07-29: an OpenStreetMap node individually named "Kasterlinde" (this entry's exact tree name, not just a street or landmark match) sits 15m from the prior anchor, at 50.8557989, 4.2898155. Treated as a surveyed point for the tree itself rather than another nearby anchor, since the node's name is the tree, not a building or street.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Parc Leopold

location.address: Parc Leopold, Rue Belliard, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: The thickest tree of its kind anywhere in Brussels stands in a park built over a vanished stream. This oriental plane, measured at 6.48 metres around in 2023, only joined the region's legal heritage inventory in August 2024, a formal recognition that arrived roughly two centuries after the tree itself. Plane trees have marked water since antiquity, when Greeks planted them by springs and wells to shade travellers, and this one keeps the tradition without anyone intending it to: the Maelbeek stream still runs underground nearby, beneath the Chaussee d'Etterbeek, and a small tower at the foot of the park's hill once operated as a 17th century fishery pond house long before the plane tree existed. At around 33 metres tall with a crown spreading 38 metres wide, the tree now shades a park built in the 1850s around a private estate, later absorbed into the district that today surrounds the European Parliament. It is, by circumference, the largest specimen of its species in the entire Brussels-Capital Region, a two hundred year old tree standing quietly behind institutions considerably younger than it is.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Metro to Maelbeek or Schuman, short walk
trees.notes: Circumference and 2024 legal inventory listing corroborated by the official heritage inventory; monumentaltrees.com used for cross-check only, per hard rule 1, not copied. Photo verified on Commons, captioned in French as this exact tree: 'notable tree, bicentennial oriental plane, Parc Leopold, Brussels'.

trees.name: The Pond Oaks and Beeches of the Bois de la Cambre

best_time.label: late October, when the beech turn copper over the ponds

location.address: Bois de la Cambre, near the ponds and Chalet Robinson, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: Brussels' most fashionable park is also a fragment of a forest older than the city walls that once surrounded it. When Leopold II's landscapers carved the Bois de la Cambre out of the northern edge of the Sonian Forest in 1861 and 1862, connecting it to the city centre by the new Avenue Louise, they left much of the existing tree cover standing rather than replanting from scratch. Around its ponds today grow pedunculate oaks, beeches, wild cherries and Austrian black pines old enough that more than eighty of them made Brussels' own official inventory of remarkable trees, out of roughly seventy such specimens spread across the whole 124 hectare park. None of these individual pond side trees carries a documented planting date of its own, so no single age is claimed here, only that they are old growth remnants of a much larger woodland: the Sonian Forest continues south from this same tree line, and a separate, strictly protected 270 hectare section of it further out was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2017 for its ancient beech stands, a reminder of what this park was cut from rather than a claim about this particular corner of it.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram to the Bois de la Cambre terminus
trees.notes: Presented deliberately as an ensemble, not one dated specimen: no individual tree here has a documented planting date. The UNESCO designation applies to a separate, protected 270 hectare section of the wider Sonian Forest, not to Bois de la Cambre itself; the story is careful to say so rather than implying this park is inside the listed zone. Photo shows the pond and Chalet Robinson area framed by mature deciduous canopy, a fair representative shot for this ensemble entry.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Parc de Woluwe

location.address: Parc de Woluwe, near Avenue de Tervueren, 1150 Woluwe-Saint-Pierre, Brussels

trees.story: The single largest tree in Brussels by trunk girth is not native to Europe at all. This giant sequoia, measured at 8.66 metres around in 2017, thicker than any other tree recorded in the region, grows in a park that did not exist until the 1890s, when the landscape architect Emile Laine laid it out for Leopold II as a green corridor linking the 1897 World's Fair site at the Cinquantenaire to a second exhibition site at Tervuren. That makes the sequoia, at most, only a little over a century old, remarkable for how much girth a genuinely young tree can put on: giant sequoias can live two thousand years and more in their native California, and reach 50 to 60 metres even in Belgium's cooler, wetter climate. Planted as an ornamental statement piece for an international exposition rather than surviving from an older forest, it has spent barely a tenth of its natural lifespan reaching a size that would take most Belgian native species several centuries to match. The park around it now holds some 180 different tree species, and this one is, by a wide margin, the thickest of all of them.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram to Parc de Woluwe, or bus from Montgomery metro station
trees.notes: Girth (866cm, measured 2017) and 'largest tree in Brussels' claim corroborated by the official heritage inventory and the park's own design history (Laine, 1890s, for Leopold II). Exact planting year not found, so age is inferred from the park's founding decade. Pin corrected 2026-07-26: the prior coordinate was about 1.1km away, outside the tree's actual position. Bruxelles Environnement's own managed-tree WFS layer (ows.environnement.brussels/green) has exactly one Sequoiadendron giganteum in the park with a circumference this large (840cm, close to this entry's own sourced 866cm within plausible remeasurement drift); a second, much smaller sequoia (503cm) also exists in the park but is clearly not 'the single largest tree in Brussels' this entry describes.

trees.name: The Purple Beech of Parc Tournay-Solvay

best_time.label: April and May, when the new leaves are brightest red-purple

location.address: Parc Tournay-Solvay, Chaussee de La Hulpe, 1170 Watermael-Boitsfort, Brussels

trees.story: Alfred Solvay, brother of the industrial chemist Ernest Solvay, built a country manor at the edge of the Sonian Forest in 1878, and the park around it still carries his family's name today. His daughter Therese Tournay-Solvay later expanded the grounds, and in the early 20th century the landscape architect Jules Buyssens redesigned them into the layout that survives now, mixing exotic plantings with remnants of the original forest vegetation. Among the survivors is a purple beech, its almost black red foliage a deliberate contrast against the ordinary green beeches nearby, part of a group of large trees in the park old enough that several, this one included, appear in the official inventory of the Brussels region's natural heritage. No source gives this specific tree an individual age, only that trees of its kind in the park run from roughly a century and a half to two centuries old, a range wide enough to be honest rather than precise. The park sits directly against the edge of the Sonian Forest in Watermael-Boitsfort, free to enter, and considerably quieter than Brussels' larger, better known green spaces.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Bus to Chaussee de La Hulpe, Watermael-Boitsfort
trees.notes: Age range (150-200 years) is sourced to the park's trees generally, not confirmed for this individual purple beech specifically; flagged as an estimate rather than a measurement. Pin corrected 2026-07-26 via Bruxelles Environnement's managed-tree WFS layer: the only Fagus sylvatica 'Atropunicea' (the purple beech cultivar) recorded in the park, moved about 500m from the prior estimate.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of the Hippodrome

location.address: Hippodrome de Boitsfort, Chaussee de La Hulpe, 1170 Watermael-Boitsfort, Brussels

trees.story: The tallest tree in Brussels grows on what used to be a racecourse. This Douglas fir, standing 33 metres, took root sometime after 1875, the year the City of Brussels leased roughly 25 hectares of forest edge to the Royal Society for the Improvement of Horse Breeds, which built a hippodrome with two grandstands here by 1878. The species itself could not have grown here any earlier: Douglas fir only reached Europe from the American Pacific coast in 1827, brought back by the Scottish botanist after whom it is named, so even the oldest possible specimen anywhere in Belgium falls short of two centuries. This one, rising above a racecourse that operated for well over a century before closing to horses, has had roughly a century and a half at most to outclimb every native species around it, and its height, not its age, is the record it holds. The hippodrome grounds are now being redeveloped as a mixed public park and university site, and the tree, along with much of the surrounding tree cover, is intended to stay exactly where it is through that transition.
trees.access: Free, public park (former racecourse, under redevelopment)
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Boitsfort, short walk
trees.notes: A source describing the hippodrome mentions some trees on the wider grounds are over 250 years old; that figure cannot apply to the Douglas fir itself, since the species was only introduced to Europe in 1827, so this entry's age range is capped accordingly and the 250 year figure is not repeated here to avoid a biologically impossible claim.

trees.name: The Sophora of the Abbaye de la Cambre

best_time.label: August, when it is one of the last trees in the city to flower

location.address: Jardins de l'Abbaye de la Cambre, Avenue Emile Duray, 1050 Ixelles, Brussels

trees.story: A Japanese pagoda tree grows in the garden of a monastery that housed Cistercian nuns for nearly six hundred years. The Abbaye de la Cambre was founded in 1201 and suppressed in 1796 during the French occupation, and while its oldest surviving stonework, the abbey church and parts of the cloister, dates to the 13th and 14th centuries, most of the garden layout around this tree is 18th century. The sophora itself is considerably younger than any of that, a species that only reached European gardens in the mid 1700s and was slower still to become a common ornamental choice, but its trunk, measured at 3.08 metres around in 2012, makes it the sixth largest of its kind recorded anywhere in the Brussels region. Light, almost feathery foliage sets it apart from the abbey's heavier, older trees, and in late summer it produces long fleshy seed pods rather than the flowers most people expect from an ornamental tree. The abbey buildings now house a school and municipal offices, but the gardens remain open to the public, free, in the middle of Ixelles.
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Tram to Abbaye or Bois de la Cambre stop
trees.notes: Girth and regional size ranking (6th largest of its species) sourced to the official heritage inventory; no planting date found for this specific tree, so age range is a broad estimate. Pin resolved 2026-07-27 via Bruxelles Environnement's managed-tree WFS: of three Sophora japonica within the abbey grounds bounding box (208cm, 330cm and 313cm circumference), the 313cm specimen is a tight match for this entry's own sourced 308cm (2012) measurement, close enough to reflect a few years' further growth. Moved about 700m to the exact match, a real correction, not just tightening.

trees.name: The Black Mulberry of the Botanical Garden

best_time.label: August, when the fruit drops and stains the path

location.address: Jardin Botanique (Le Botanique), Rue Royale, 1210 Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, Brussels

trees.story: A mulberry tree possibly older than Belgium itself grows in a garden that predates the country by four years. The State Botanical Garden of Brussels opened on this site in 1826, on a 6.4 hectare terraced plot at the corner of what is now Rue Royale and the Boulevard du Jardin Botanique, and this black mulberry, its trunk over two metres around, is old enough that it plausibly dates to those original 1820s plantings, though no surviving record names its exact planting year. Black mulberry is a Mediterranean species, slow to fruit and famous for staining anything beneath it a deep purple black when its berries drop in late summer, a domestic habit that made it a fixture of European monastery and manor gardens for centuries before this one arrived in a public botanical collection. The garden itself stopped functioning as a working scientific collection decades ago and is now a public park known simply as Le Botanique, its 19th century glasshouse repurposed as a concert venue, but the trees planted for research have stayed exactly where the botanists left them.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Metro to Botanique, 2 min walk
trees.notes: No source gives this tree a confirmed planting date; the 1826 garden founding date is used as a plausible upper bound, not a documented fact about this specific mulberry, and the story states that caveat directly. Pin resolved 2026-07-27 via Bruxelles Environnement's own managed-tree WFS (ows.environnement.brussels/green, layer 'tree', the same source used for bru_005/bru_006 on 2026-07-26): exactly one Morus nigra recorded within Le Botanique's grounds (id_arb 20337), circumference 265cm, matching this entry's own sourced 'over two metres around' almost exactly. Moved about 100m to the exact match.

trees.name: The Chestnut Avenue of the Cinquantenaire

best_time.label: May, when its candle-shaped flowers bloom along the avenue

location.address: Parc du Cinquantenaire, 1000 Brussels / 1040 Etterbeek

trees.story: When Brussels built Parc du Cinquantenaire in 1880 to mark Belgium's fiftieth year as a country, it cheated on the trees. Rather than planting saplings and waiting decades for a new park to look established, city gardeners transplanted trees that were already fully grown, moved in from the old Leopold Quarter cemetery, the Bois de la Cambre and the edge of the Sonian Forest itself. The common horse chestnuts that line one of the park's principal avenues are among the clearest survivors of that trick: mature when they arrived, they are older than the park itself by however many decades they had already grown before the move, plausibly close to two centuries old today, though no individual planting record confirms a precise figure for any single tree in the row. Around fifteen trees across the wider Cinquantenaire park made it onto Brussels' official register of remarkable trees, chestnuts among them alongside false acacias, a silver maple and a rare Italian alder, but the chestnut avenue is the one most visitors walk beneath without knowing they are standing under trees older than the triumphal arch at the park's centre.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Metro to Schuman or Merode, short walk
trees.notes: The transplanting story (mature trees moved from the old Leopold Quarter cemetery, Bois de la Cambre and the Sonian Forest when the park was built in 1880) is well corroborated, but no individual chestnut in the avenue has a confirmed age; the range given assumes a plausible age at transplanting plus the 146 years since 1880. Photo shows a tree-lined avenue in Cinquantenaire/Jubelpark, a fair representative shot for this ensemble entry. Pin tightened 2026-07-27 via Bruxelles Environnement's managed-tree WFS: 11 Aesculus hippocastanum recorded across the park's grounds, consistent with the source's count of about fifteen registered remarkable trees there; moved about 210m to the centroid of that cluster, the same honest-ensemble treatment as Amsterdam's Amstelveld wingnuts.

trees.name: The Turner's Oak of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, by the palace railings at the end of the Passage de Milan, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: Every register starts somewhere, and Brussels started here. When the region opened its scientific inventory of remarkable trees, this squat evergreen oak was the first entry made, in 1999, ahead of every giant sequoia and four hundred year old oak that has been added since. It earned the place without being old or tall. It stands ten metres high and spreads its crown seventeen metres wide, a shape that reads more like a parasol than a tree, and its trunk is 2.90 metres around, second thickest of its kind in the whole region. Turner's oak is a garden invention rather than a wild species, a cross between the common pedunculate oak and the Mediterranean holm oak raised in an Essex nursery and named after the nurseryman who raised it. It kept the southern parent's leathery leaves, so it stays green through a Brussels winter and only goes briefly bare in spring when the new growth pushes the old leaves off, the reverse of every other oak around it. The landscape architect Edmond Galoppin most likely planted it when he remade these palace gardens as an English park in 1901. A second, taller Turner's oak grows a few minutes away on the same lawns.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily 08:00 to 20:00
trees.transport: Metro to Louise, about 5 minutes on foot through the Boulevard de Waterloo entrance
trees.notes: Girth 290cm measured 2019, height 10m, crown 17m, health recorded as 'Sain', and the ranking as second thickest of its species in the region all come from the region's own per-tree record (heritage.brussels tree 648, legally inventoried 19 August 2024). The 1999 first-entry fact and the Galoppin 1901 planting attribution come from Wood Wide Web, Brussels Environment's published tree atlas, which gives a GPS reading of 50.8381, 4.3577 for this tree, matching the register coordinate exactly. Wood Wide Web's own card mixes this tree's data with the park's second Turner's oak (register 649, 264cm, 23m tall), so only the figures confirmed by the register are used here. Age is inferred from the 1901 park remaking rather than a planting record, hence the range. Wood Wide Web dates the hybrid's creation to the late 19th century, which conflicts with the standard account of an 18th century Essex origin, so the story names the nursery and the parentage but claims no date. No open licensed photograph of this individual tree found: heritage.brussels publishes photographs of it but states no licence beyond a blanket site copyright, and Wikimedia Commons has park views only, none identifiable as this tree.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Parc d'Egmont

best_time.label: November, when it drops the whole crown of gold in a few days

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the lawn facing the Egmont Palace railings, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: This ginkgo is being slowly harmed by people who like it. It is the seventh thickest of its species recorded anywhere in the Brussels region, 3.27 metres around and twenty metres tall, and it stands on open grass in the only public park inside the old city walls that sits entirely in the middle of a block, invisible from every street around it. That makes it the obvious place to lie down on a warm afternoon, and enough people have lain under this particular tree that the soil over its roots is packed hard, which is why the region's surveyors record its condition as slightly defective despite it being, for a ginkgo, extremely young. Ginkgos are the last survivors of a lineage that was already ancient when the first flowering plants appeared, and they are famous for shrugging off pollution, disease and radiation. Compacted ground is the one thing they do not shrug off. The reward for keeping a couple of metres back is in November, when the fan shaped leaves turn a uniform butter gold and then let go almost all at once, laying a circle of yellow on the grass. A walnut across the lawn turns at the same time, so the whole clearing goes yellow together.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily 08:00 to 20:00
trees.transport: Metro to Louise, about 5 minutes on foot through the Boulevard de Waterloo entrance
trees.notes: Girth 327cm measured 2019, height 20m, crown 18m and the health rating 'Legers defauts' come from the region's per-tree record (heritage.brussels tree 637, legally inventoried 19 August 2024). The soil compaction diagnosis and the paired autumn colour with the walnut opposite come from Wood Wide Web (atlas 3698), Brussels Environment's published tree atlas, whose GPS reading of 50.8383, 4.3567 lands within about 5 metres of the register coordinate. The two sources disagree by one place on the regional size ranking, sixth on Wood Wide Web against seventh on the register; the register's own figure is used. No planting record exists, so the age follows the park's 1901 remaking under Edmond Galoppin. No open licensed photograph of this individual tree found.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Parc d'Egmont

best_time.label: June, when the tulip flowers open high in the crown

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, beside the ginkgo on the palace lawn, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: In autumn 2018 a Brussels art institute adopted this tree. The ISELP, whose building stands a few streets away, chose the tulip tree of Parc d'Egmont as the living centrepiece of an exhibition called A Forest, on the argument that a monument you can walk around, in a park that joins the upper and lower city, does something a gallery wall cannot: it makes a passerby slow down. The tree is a good candidate for the job. It is 3.06 metres around and twenty seven metres tall, the only specimen on this list the region's surveyors record as being in outright good health, and it carries the strangest leaf in the park, cut off flat at the tip as though someone had trimmed it with scissors. Its flowers are the reason for the name and the reason most people miss them: greenish yellow, tulip shaped, and produced high in the crown in June, where they sit above eye level until a storm drops one on the path. Europeans wanted this American tree so badly in the eighteenth century that its seeds were smuggled. Three hundred years later the enthusiasm has come back around, in the form of an art exhibition.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily 08:00 to 20:00
trees.transport: Metro to Louise, about 5 minutes on foot through the Boulevard de Waterloo entrance
trees.notes: Girth 306cm measured 2019, height 27m, crown 20m, health 'Sain' and the ranking of nineteenth thickest of its species in the region come from heritage.brussels tree 642, legally inventoried 19 August 2024. The ISELP sponsorship during the exhibition A Forest, 21 September to 15 December 2018, and the eighteenth century seed trade are recorded on Wood Wide Web (atlas 154), Brussels Environment's published tree atlas, whose GPS reading of 50.8381, 4.3567 lands within about 5 metres of the register coordinate. Wood Wide Web files this tree under the address Boulevard de Waterloo 31, which is the park's street entrance rather than a separate location. No planting record exists, so the age follows the park's 1901 remaking under Edmond Galoppin. No open licensed photograph of this individual tree found.

trees.name: The Great Sycamore of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the western lawns near the Rue aux Laines side, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: Nobody plants a sycamore on purpose any more. It seeds itself into gutters and railway banks across Europe, grows fast, and gets cut down long before it can become anything, which is what makes the largest tree in this park worth looking up at: 32 metres of it, with a clean trunk running six metres before the first branch and a girth of 3.97 metres measured in 2026. The region's surveyors rank it the third thickest sycamore recorded anywhere in Brussels. It is also the reason the park feels bigger than its one and a half hectares. Parc d'Egmont is sealed on all four sides by buildings, the only public green space inside the old city walls with no street frontage at all, and a tree this tall pushes the sense of the place upward instead of outward. The sycamore has been in Belgium so long that most people take it for a native, though it arrived from the mountains of central Europe centuries ago and settled in as thoroughly as any local species. Its winged seeds spin down in September in numbers that would fill the whole park with seedlings if the gardeners let them.

best_time.label: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.access: Free, public park, open daily 08:00 to 20:00
trees.transport: Metro to Louise, about 5 minutes on foot through the Rue aux Laines or Boulevard de Waterloo entrance
trees.notes: Girth 397cm measured in 2026, height 32m, crown 20m, bole 6m, health 'Legers defauts' and the ranking of third thickest of its species in the region come from heritage.brussels tree 6357, legally inventoried 19 August 2024. This is the freshest measurement of any tree in the cluster. Flagged on age: no source dates this tree, and its girth is large enough that it may predate the 1901 Galoppin remaking and belong to Tilman-Francois Suys' 1830 layout instead, so the range is deliberately wide. Deliberately claims no height record: brussels.json already credits the Douglas Fir of the Hippodrome as the tallest tree in the city at 33m, and this one is a metre short of that, so only the species-level girth ranking is claimed. trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, at the southern edge against the Rue du Grand Cerf gardens, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: This cedar has spent its life pretending to be a broadleaf. Instead of the single straight column its species normally builds, its trunk divides low down into two enormous limbs, one leaning out over the back gardens of the Rue du Grand Cerf, the other reaching into the wooded corner of the park, and the resulting silhouette looks far more like an old beech than a conifer. Walk up to it and the disguise fails immediately: the resin smell is unmistakable, the needles come in tight rosettes rather than singly, and the cones sit upright on the branches like small barrels with their scales pressed flat. It measures 2.98 metres around and stands at the park's boundary rather than on its lawns, half visible from the street, which is probably why it is the least photographed of the park's registered trees. Cedars of Lebanon reached western European gardens in the seventeenth century, and the estates that could afford them planted them as statements. This one has outlived the statement. The palace beside it burned in 1892 and was rebuilt, the gardens were redrawn twice, the city bought the whole thing in 1918, and the cedar carried on splitting itself in two directions.

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.name: The Red Oak of Parc d'Egmont

best_time.label: October, when it turns scarlet a few weeks before the ginkgo turns gold

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, across the path from the ginkgo, 1000 Brussels

trees.story: Brussels Environment's own walking route through this park gives up on describing this tree and simply says that in autumn you will notice it before you read the sign. That is fair. The northern red oak turns a deep scarlet that no European oak can produce, holds it for a couple of weeks in October, and does it here about a month before the ginkgo thirty metres away goes gold, so the same clearing performs twice in one season. The tree measures 3.42 metres around and reaches 24 metres, with a crown eighteen metres across. Its leaves are the easiest identification in the park: broad, thin, with bristle tipped points at the end of every lobe, nothing like the rounded lobes of the pedunculate oaks Belgium grows natively. It comes from eastern North America, where it is a forest tree rather than a park specimen, and it arrived in European gardens in the eighteenth century as a novelty that grew faster than anything local. Faster growth is also why it has never reached the age of a real veteran oak here, and why it is a middle aged tree that already looks substantial.

trees.name: The London Plane of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the lawns below the Rue aux Laines side, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
The second thickest tree in this park ranks ninety eighth of its species across Brussels, which says more about the city than about the tree. The region has measured so many big London planes that a trunk 3.67 metres round barely places, and this one still holds a crown twenty metres wide over the Egmont lawns with only the great sycamore beating it for girth.

The London plane is a hybrid nobody planned. An oriental plane and an American plane crossed in a European garden in the seventeenth century and produced a tree tougher than either parent, which went on to line more streets than anything else on the continent. It tolerates compacted roots, drought and filthy air, and it sheds its bark in plates, which is the habit that keeps it looking clean in a city that is not.

The setting is the odd part. Parc d'Egmont is a hectare and a half boxed in on every side by the buildings of the Sablon, entered through passages rather than gates, which is how a tree this size stands five minutes from the Avenue Louise and stays unknown to people who shop there weekly.

Brussels' legal inventory records the girth and the crown for this one, and, unusually for a register this thorough, no height at all.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the western lawns, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
The horse chestnut is one of the most planted trees in Europe and one of the rarest in the wild. Its entire natural range is a scatter of mountain ravines in northern Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, a few thousand trees in gorges, out of which sixteenth century collectors carried it to Istanbul, then to Vienna, then to everywhere. Conkers turned it into a children's institution across a continent; the wild population is small enough to be listed as threatened.

This one is 3.08 metres round with a crown fifteen metres across, on lawns closed in on all sides by the buildings of the Sablon. Brussels ranks it ninetieth of its species in the region, which for a tree this common is a respectable place to sit.

Being planted everywhere has cost it. Since the 1990s the horse chestnut leaf miner has spread across Europe, a moth whose larvae tunnel the leaves until they brown and curl by August, so most chestnuts on the continent now look half dead two months before autumn without actually being ill. Bleeding canker is the serious one, and the one that kills.

The flowers go up like white candles in May. The conkers come down in late September, which is the only fortnight of the year anybody looks at the ground under this tree.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, signposted on the park's information panel, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
Seventy metres separate this tree from its own hybrid offspring. The oriental plane is one of the two parents of the London plane, and both grow in Parc d'Egmont within sight of each other, the parent 2.72 metres round and the descendant 3.67, which is roughly how that cross behaves everywhere: faster, tougher, thicker than the tree it came from.

Platanus orientalis is the plane of the eastern Mediterranean, the tree of Greek market squares and Persian gardens, the species Hippocrates is said to have taught under on Kos and the one Xerxes reportedly stopped his army to hang with gold. It differs from its descendant in the leaf, cut far more deeply into narrow lobes, and in temperament: it wants water and warmth, and grows slowly when it does not get them.

This one stands twenty two metres with a crown twelve metres across, and the park's own information panel names it, which most of the 582 trees on the region's legal inventory never get. Brussels ranks it twenty first of its species.

The regional champion is a kilometre and a half east in Parc Leopold, the thickest oriental plane recorded anywhere in the city, which is a fair reason to walk between the two.

trees.name: The Kentucky Coffeetree of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, near the Passage de Milan end, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
In Dutch this tree is the doodsbeenderenboom, the dead men's bones tree. The name is about its winter. The Kentucky coffeetree comes into leaf later than almost anything else in a Belgian park, often not before late May, drops early in autumn, and spends the months between as a set of thick blunt grey twigs with nothing on them, which somebody once decided looked like bones.

It sits on Brussels' legal register of remarkable trees at a girth of seventy three centimetres, which is nothing, and it is still the fourth largest of its kind in the region. That is a comment on Brussels rather than on this tree. Gymnocladus dioica grows wild in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, is uncommon even there, and Europe has never planted it in any quantity.

The common name comes from settlers in Kentucky who roasted and ground the seeds as a coffee substitute. The roasting mattered: raw, the seeds and pods are toxic. The species is dioecious, which is what the dioica means, so male and female flowers grow on separate trees and only a female sets the heavy leathery pods.

It is a young tree with a six metre crown, here for the botany rather than the spectacle, and worth two minutes on the way to the sycamore.

https://sites.heritage.brussels/fr/trees/7112 (the region's per-tree record, which ranks it fourth largest of its species in the Brussels-Capital Region)

trees.name: The Second Turner's Oak of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, near the Passage de Milan end, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
Parc d'Egmont has two Turner's oaks, and the region's own tree atlas has spent years quietly mixing up their measurements. This is the taller and thicker of the pair, 264 centimetres around and 23 metres high, against the other tree's 10 metres. Both are the same garden hybrid, bred in an English nursery by crossing the common pedunculate oak with the evergreen Mediterranean holm oak, which is why both keep their leathery leaves through a Brussels winter and only drop them briefly in spring when new growth pushes the old ones off.

Brussels region's inventory of remarkable trees lists this one as the third thickest of its kind anywhere in the region, ranked by an official survey rather than a guess. No planting date survives for it specifically, though the palace grounds around it were remade as an English landscape park in 1901 by Edmond Galoppin, the likely era for both oaks even without a record naming either one.

The two trees stand a few minutes' walk apart on the same lawns, which makes them an easy pair to see together: the smaller, older-registered oak near the palace railings, this taller one closer to the Passage de Milan gate.

trees.name: The White Mulberries of the Passage de Milan Gate

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, flanking the Passage de Milan gate, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
A pair of white mulberries flanks the Passage de Milan gate into Parc d'Egmont, one on each side, thick enough that the region's own tree inventory ranks the pair among the eighth-thickest of their species anywhere in Brussels. White mulberry is a different tree from the black mulberry Brussels already protects at the Botanical Garden: paler bark, sweeter and blander fruit, and a species grown across Europe for centuries not for eating but for its leaves, the only food silkworms will reliably take.

Neither tree has a documented planting date. What is certain is the pair itself, planted close enough to read as a matched set marking an entrance rather than as two unrelated trees that happened to end up near each other, and a trunk girth of 130 centimetres each that puts them well past a garden sapling's age.

Mulberries fruit in July, dark and staining when ripe, and a public park pair like this one rarely gets to keep its harvest: birds strip a mulberry fast. Free to walk past at any hour, on the same lawns as the park's two Turner's oaks and its ginkgo.

trees.name: The Turkish Hazel of the Grand Sablon

location.address: Place du Grand Sablon, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
The Grand Sablon is better known for its antiques market and its chocolate shops than for a tree, which is exactly why the Turkish hazel standing in it is easy to walk past. The region's official inventory of remarkable trees ranks it eleventh of its species anywhere in Brussels, 17 metres tall with a 16 metre crown and a trunk 208 centimetres around, recorded as fully healthy and holding, in the register's own words, a central position in the square's landscape.

Turkish hazel is the one hazel that grows as a proper tree rather than a multi-stemmed shrub, with a straight trunk and a tidy, pyramidal crown that made it a favourite for European city squares long before anyone thought to protect individual specimens. It flowers in late winter, small and easy to miss, and carries its nuts through summer inside a spiky husk that looks nothing like a supermarket hazelnut.

Only the official register documents this specific tree so far, which is stated here rather than smoothed over. What the register gives is precise and consistent (rank, dimensions, a health check), which is a different kind of confidence than a second written source, and one this page is honest about.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Mont des Arts

location.address: Jardin du Mont des Arts, Brussels

trees.story:
The Mont des Arts garden is not what it looks like: a formal, two-hectare terrace of clipped yew and box hedges offering one of the best panoramic views over central Brussels, it is actually a roof, built in 1957 to 1958 over an underground car park, designed by the Belgian landscape architect Rene Pechere as what the profession calls a suspended garden. This pedunculate oak, girthed at 166 centimetres and legally inscribed on the region's official remarkable-trees register, grows in that engineered ground between the Royal Library and the Avenue des Arts.

The site's own history goes back further than the garden itself: an earlier version was laid out for the 1910 World's Fair to hide, in the words of its own French landscape architect Jules Vacherot, the shabby state of the hillside beneath a cloak of greenery and flowers. What stands today is the second attempt at the same idea, decades later and considerably more ambitious. Brussels' official inventory records the oak's girth and legal status without a planting date, so the tree's age is undocumented rather than estimated. It grows in the open, free, on one of the city's most photographed viewpoints.

best_time.label: September and October, when the acorns drop and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Ailanthus of Mont des Arts

location.address: Near the Jardin du Mont des Arts, Brussels

trees.story:
Most cities that have a Tree of Heaven at all have one nobody planted, since Ailanthus altissima spreads through cracked pavement and vacant lots so readily that it is treated as a weed across much of Europe and North America. This one is different: girthed at 321 centimetres, one of the widest trunks on this whole list, and formally inscribed on the region's legal register of remarkable trees, a species usually pulled out on sight given a rare pass because of its size and standing.

It grows near the Mont des Arts, the raised garden terrace between Brussels' upper and lower town, built over an underground car park in the 1950s on a site that has carried some form of ornamental greenery since the 1910 World's Fair. Ailanthus was imported to Europe from China in the 18th century as an ornamental curiosity and a potential silk-moth host before anyone anticipated how aggressively it would naturalise; a specimen this large and this old getting protected status rather than removed is the exception rather than the rule. It stands free, in the open, a short walk from the garden's oak and its Caucasian wingnut.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Mont des Arts

location.address: Near the Jardin du Mont des Arts, Brussels

trees.story:
Caucasian wingnut takes its name from what it does with its seeds rather than what it looks like: long, pendulous strings of winged fruit that hang from the branches through late summer, an unmistakable trait for a tree most visitors would otherwise mistake for an oversized walnut. Native to the forests of the western Caucasus, it reached European gardens in the early 19th century as one of many exotic imports that formal city gardens across the continent competed to acquire.

This specimen, girthed at 173 centimetres with a 13 metre crown, is legally inscribed on Brussels' official register of remarkable trees and grows near the Mont des Arts, the raised terrace garden between the city's upper and lower halves, built over an underground car park in the 1950s. The species suckers readily from its roots, often forming small groves rather than single trunks in the wild, though this one is recorded and protected as an individual specimen. It stands in the open, free, on a short walk that also takes in the garden's oak and its far larger ailanthus.

best_time.label: high summer, when long strings of winged fruit hang from every branch

trees.name: The Pyramidal Holly of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the western lawns towards the Rue aux Laines side, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
Holly is a hedge in most of Brussels, and a sprig on a card in December. Left uncut it becomes a tree, and this is what that looks like: a trunk 1.40 metres round on the western lawns of Parc d'Egmont, which the region's inventory of remarkable trees ranks as the second largest of its cultivar anywhere in Brussels.

The cultivar is 'Pyramidalis', a narrow, upright selection of the common European holly. A cultivar is not something that turns up in a wood and comes back true from seed. Every 'Pyramidalis' is a cutting of a cutting of one original plant, so this tree and the ones standing in gardens elsewhere in Europe are the same individual, grown on in different soil.

Holly lays down wood very slowly, which is the whole reason 140 centimetres earns a place on an official register while the sycamore on the same lawn carries 397 centimetres and ranks only third of its kind. Nobody has dated this one and the register does not try. It measures, it ranks, and it leaves the years alone. If you know the park's planting records, we would take the correction.

The park signposts it on its own panel, which spares you the hunt: at a distance a holly this size still reads as a shrub, right up until you are close enough to see the trunk.

trees.name: The Pagoda Tree of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the lawns towards the Passage de Milan gate, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
Brussels files this tree under a name and a nationality that are both wrong. The register lists it as Sophora japonica. Botanists moved the species to Styphnolobium some time ago and most registers have not caught up, and it was never Japanese in the first place: it is native to China and Korea, and reached Europe by way of Japanese gardens, which is how it collected an epithet that has now outlived two corrections.

In China it was the tree of the imperial court, planted at palaces and tombs, and by tradition it was a pagoda tree on Coal Hill in Beijing that the last Ming emperor hanged himself from in 1644, with rebel armies already inside the city.

This one is a quieter proposition. Surveyors walked Parc d'Egmont in July 2019 and entered it on the region's inventory of remarkable trees, where it ranks inside the top thirty of its species for Brussels. There are not many to rank. The pagoda tree has never been planted here in quantity, which is exactly how a specimen of no great size ends up on an official list.

That survey logged one point on the lawns for the trees it added rather than a coordinate per trunk, so the pin puts you in the right corner of a park you can cross in three minutes and no closer. Nobody has recorded its age.

best_time.label: late summer, when it flowers cream white in the weeks almost nothing else does

trees.how_to_recognise: Light, open, pinnate foliage on a modest trunk, on the lawns towards the Passage de Milan gate. The pin is the survey's shared point for three trees rather than this trunk, so expect to look around once you are through the gate.

trees.name: The Weeping Ash of Parc d'Egmont

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the lawns towards the Passage de Milan gate, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
A weeping ash has no top of its own. The weeping habit is a mutation that will not throw a leading shoot, so these trees are almost always grafted onto the head of an ordinary ash stem: the trunk rises as far as the grafter's join and then stops, and everything above it falls back down in a dome. Find the change in the bark somewhere around head height and you are looking at the seam between two different plants.

This one grows on the lawns of Parc d'Egmont and went onto the region's inventory of remarkable trees after a survey in July 2019. It ranks inside the top thirty of its kind recorded in Brussels.

The species underneath the graft is having a bad century. Ash dieback, a fungus out of east Asia, has worked its way across Belgium over the past fifteen years and killed ash trees at a rate European forestry has no answer to. Nobody can promise what that means for this one, which is an argument for going to look at it rather than against.

The July survey logged a single coordinate for the trees it added rather than one per trunk, so the pin marks the group and not this stem. No age is recorded, here or anywhere: the inventory measures and ranks, and lets the years alone.

trees.name: The Thornless Honey Locust of Parc d'Egmont
trees.species: Thornless Honey Locust (Gleditsia triacanthos var. inermis)

location.address: Parc d'Egmont, on the lawns towards the Passage de Milan gate, 1000 Brussels

trees.story:
The inermis on this tree's register entry means unarmed, and it is doing a lot of work. A wild honey locust grows branched spikes straight out of its own trunk, up to twenty centimetres long and hard enough to go through a tyre, which is why the thornless form is the only one anybody puts in a city park.

The usual explanation for those spikes is that they are about thirteen thousand years out of date. They are sized for animals that no longer exist, the giant ground sloths and mastodons that browsed North American woodland until the end of the last ice age, ate the tree's long twisted pods for the sweet pulp inside and carried the seed off in their guts. The pods still drop every autumn. Now they rot where they land.

Surveyors entered this specimen on the region's inventory of remarkable trees after a pass through Parc d'Egmont in July 2019, and it sits inside the top thirty of its species for Brussels. None of the three trees that survey added is big: the thickest of them measures 164 centimetres round.

The survey gave one coordinate for the group instead of a pin per tree, so the exact spot inside the park is not on record. Look for the finest leaves in Egmont, leaflets small enough that the shade under a honey locust is barely shade. Nobody has dated it.
